section.title: The Lord Is My Shepherd
section.sectionRationale: The best known and most beloved psalm in the Psalter, David's picture of the LORD as shepherd shifts midway from speaking about God, 'He', to speaking directly to Him, 'You', at the moment of deepest danger, the valley of the shadow of death. Its imagery of green pastures, a shepherd's rod and staff, a prepared table, and dwelling forever in God's house is fulfilled in Jesus, who names Himself the good shepherd in John 10.
section.thesis: David's confidence that the LORD is his shepherd, providing, guiding, and protecting him even through the valley of the shadow of death, is fulfilled completely in Jesus Christ, the good shepherd who lays down His life for His sheep.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the shepherd's provision in green pastures and quiet waters; the shift to direct address in the valley of the shadow of death, fearless because You are with me; and the closing picture of a prepared table and a home in the LORD's house forever.

verses.text: The LORD is my {{roeh|shepherd}}; I shall not want.
He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters.

He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness 
for the sake of His name.

units.label: I will fear no evil, for You are with me
units.note: the shift to direct address in the valley

verses.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.

units.label: I will dwell in the house of the Lord forever
units.note: a prepared table and an everlasting home

verses.text: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.
Surely goodness and {{chesed|mercy}} will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.

roeh.gloss: Shepherd, one who tends, feeds, and guides a flock. The image draws on David's own early life tending sheep and on Israel's long tradition of describing God, and Israel's kings, as shepherds of the people, fulfilled completely in Jesus, the good shepherd, John 10:11.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion, rendered here 'mercy' or 'lovingkindness.' David pictures this loyal love as actively pursuing him, following him, all the days of his life, not a distant attitude but an active, pursuing presence.

basic.context: David pictures God as a shepherd who provides everything he needs: green pastures, quiet waters, a restored soul, guidance on right paths. At the psalm's very center, the moment of greatest danger, the valley of the shadow of death, David's language shifts from talking about God, 'He leads me', to talking directly to Him, 'You are with me'. The psalm closes with a picture of a table prepared even in the presence of enemies, an anointed and overflowing welcome, and the settled hope of dwelling in God's house forever.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm's central turn, from third person description to direct, personal address exactly when danger is named, teaches something profound about faith: nearness to God is often found and felt most intensely not before or after hardship but in the very middle of it. The whole psalm should be read as personal, devotional truth meant to be prayed, not merely admired as poetry.
basic.originalLanguages: David calls the LORD his ro'eh, shepherd, an image rooted in his own early life tending sheep and in Israel's long tradition of shepherd kings. His closing confidence rests in chesed, God's covenant loving devotion, pictured here as actively pursuing him, following him, all the days of his life.
basic.typology: David's LORD as shepherd anticipates Jesus, who explicitly claims this title for Himself, the good shepherd, John 10:11, who, unlike a hired hand, lays down His life for the sheep, fulfilling and surpassing every promise of provision and protection this psalm describes.
basic.christ: Jesus directly claims the title this psalm gives to the LORD: 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep', John 10:11. Every provision David describes, rest, restoration, guided paths, fearless presence in the valley of death, a prepared table, an everlasting home, finds its fullest and final meaning in Christ, who does not merely lead sheep beside quiet waters but walks through death itself ahead of His flock and rises to prepare an eternal home for them, John 14:2-3.
basic.god: God is shown as intimately, personally involved in provision and protection, a shepherd who knows His sheep individually, and whose presence, not the absence of danger, is what removes fear even in the valley of death's shadow.
basic.crossReferences: John 10:11-15 shows Jesus claiming the title of good shepherd, laying down His life for the sheep. Ezekiel 34:11-16 pictures God Himself searching for and shepherding His scattered people. Revelation 7:17 pictures the Lamb as shepherd, guiding His people to springs of living water.
basic.oneStory: David's confidence in the LORD as his shepherd, sufficient through green pastures and the valley of death alike, finds its complete fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the good shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep and now leads all who trust Him toward an everlasting home in the Father's house.

context.literary:
Psalm 23 is a psalm of trust, and its six verses are built with great economy. The covenant name frames the whole: in Hebrew the psalm opens with 'The LORD' and closes with 'the house of the LORD,' an inclusio that sets every line inside His name.

Within that frame the psalm moves along a journey rather than resting in one scene. It passes from pasture, to water, to paths, into a dark valley, to a table, and finally to a house. The flock is always going somewhere, and the destination is the dwelling of God.

The pronouns trace the heart of the poem. Verses 1 to 3 speak about the LORD in the third person, 'He makes me lie down,' 'He leads me.' In verses 4 and 5 the singer turns to address Him, 'You are with me,' 'You prepare a table.' Verse 6 widens the lens again, 'the house of the LORD.' The words 'for You are with me' stand near the centre of the psalm, and everything before and after leans on them.

There are two governing images, the shepherd in verses 1 to 4 and the host in verses 5 and 6, though some readers hear the shepherd throughout. The lines are short and rely on Hebrew parallelism, each half line sharpening the other: pastures and waters, rod and staff, goodness and loving devotion.

Its setting in the Psalter matters. Psalm 22 opens with 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' and ends with the poor eating and being satisfied, Psalm 22:26. Psalm 24 asks, 'Who may ascend the hill of the LORD?' Psalm 23 sits between a cry of abandonment and the procession of the King of Glory into His sanctuary, and it walks the road from one to the other.
context.historical:
The superscription reads 'A Psalm of David.' David knew the shepherd's life from boyhood. He was out with the sheep when Samuel came to anoint him, 1 Samuel 16:11, and he told Saul how he struck down a lion and a bear to rescue a lamb from their mouths, 1 Samuel 17:34-35. When the tribes made him king they recalled God's word, 'You will shepherd My people Israel,' 2 Samuel 5:2, and Psalm 78:70-72 describes God taking him 'from the sheepfolds' to shepherd Jacob.

Calling a king a shepherd was common across the ancient Near East; Hammurabi of Babylon styled himself the shepherd of his people. What is striking here is that the king himself takes the place of a sheep. The shepherd king confesses that he too needs a shepherd.

Judean shepherding was hard, mobile work. Grass was seasonal and water scarce, and a shepherd had to know where the next grazing lay and lead his flock there on paths through steep, shadowed wadis where wild animals and robbers could strike. The rod was a club for defence; the staff was for guiding and steadying.

The host of verses 5 and 6 draws on the customs of hospitality. To be received at a man's table was to come under his protection, and to have one's head anointed with oil was a mark of honour to a guest, as Jesus' words to Simon the Pharisee assume, Luke 7:46. Some have linked the psalm to David's flight from Absalom, when friends met him at Mahanaim with food 'in the wilderness,' 2 Samuel 17:27-29, but the psalm names no occasion. 'The house of the LORD' need not presuppose Solomon's temple; the tabernacle at Shiloh is already called 'the house of the LORD' in 1 Samuel 1:7.
context.canonical:
The shepherd image begins long before David. Jacob blesses Joseph in the name of 'the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,' Genesis 48:15. The exodus is remembered as a shepherding: God 'led out His people like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness. He led them safely, so they did not fear,' Psalm 78:52-53. Moses prayed that Israel would not be 'like sheep without a shepherd,' Numbers 27:17.

Later psalms return to the theme. Psalm 80:1 calls on the 'Shepherd of Israel,' and Psalm 95:7 and Psalm 100:3 name Israel 'the sheep of His pasture.' The prophets take it further when Israel's human shepherds fail. Jeremiah 23:1-6 pronounces woe on the shepherds who scatter, promises that God Himself will gather the flock, and ties that promise to a righteous Branch for David. Ezekiel 34 does the same, with God declaring 'I Myself will search for My flock,' Ezekiel 34:11, and then appointing 'one shepherd, My servant David,' Ezekiel 34:23. Isaiah 40:11 pictures the returning Lord who 'tends His flock like a shepherd' and carries the lambs close to His heart.

The New Testament gathers these threads in Jesus. He has compassion on crowds who are 'like sheep without a shepherd,' Mark 6:34, echoing Numbers 27:17. He claims the title in John 10. Hebrews 13:20 calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' 1 Peter 2:25 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls,' and 1 Peter 5:4 'the Chief Shepherd.' Revelation 7:17 joins Psalm 23 to Isaiah 49:10 in the final vision: the Lamb will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wants his hearers to trust the LORD personally and completely, and he teaches that trust by confession rather than instruction. The psalm never tells anyone what to do. It says what the LORD is, 'my shepherd,' and draws the consequences: no lack, no fear, a place at His table and in His house.

He also wants Israel to read its own history into the psalm. The vocabulary of leading, guiding, resting places and a table in the wilderness is the vocabulary of the exodus, Exodus 15:13 and Psalm 78:19. What God did for the nation He does for the single worshipper, and what the worshipper confesses, the nation can sing together in the sanctuary.

Finally, David wants his hearers to know that the dark valley belongs inside the life of faith, not outside it. The psalm does not promise a route that avoids the ravine. It promises company in it, and a destination beyond it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a confession of trust, not a list of guarantees. It does not promise that believers will never be hungry, ill, pursued or bereaved; David himself knew all of these. 'I shall not want' means that the one who belongs to this Shepherd lacks nothing he truly needs to be led home, as Israel 'lacked nothing' in the wilderness even while it wandered, Deuteronomy 2:7.

What it does prescribe, by example, is a way of speaking in trouble. When danger appears, David turns from talking about God to talking to Him. Believers today are invited to take the psalm on their lips as their own, in sickness, grief and at the bedside of the dying, while reading it through the Shepherd who has fulfilled it, so that the promise of the table and the house is heard in the light of Christ.

debates.question: Does 'the valley of the shadow of death' in verse 4 mean the experience of dying, or any deep darkness?

views.label: Any valley of deep darkness
views.case: The Hebrew word, tsalmavet, may be a single word meaning deep gloom, which is why the BSB footnote offers 'the valley of deep darkness.' Jeremiah 2:6 uses it for the wilderness Israel crossed, 'a land of drought and darkness,' and a shepherd's ravine fits that range of dangers.

views.label: Death itself
views.case: The traditional vocalisation reads the word as 'shadow' plus 'death,' and it appears beside death in Job 38:17, 'the gates of the shadow of death.' The psalm's closing hope of the LORD's house, together with later revelation of resurrection, suggests its scope extends through dying.

debates.bearing: The word covers the whole range of darkness, and death is its deepest instance. The psalm's comfort is not the size of the valley but the presence of the Shepherd in it, which is why believers have rightly read it at gravesides as well as in lesser troubles.

debates.question: Is the psalm one image or two, a shepherd throughout or a shepherd who becomes a host?

views.label: Two images, shepherd and host
views.case: Tables, oil and cups belong to a household, not a pasture, so most readers see a shift at verse 5 from the field to the banquet hall. The move deepens the relationship, from being cared for as a sheep to being honoured as a guest.

views.label: One shepherd image throughout
views.case: Some argue that a shepherd prepares grazing ground, treats the heads of sheep with oil against insects and wounds, and leads the flock home to the fold, so that the whole psalm stays in the pasture.

debates.bearing: The words of verse 5, especially 'prepare a table,' echo Psalm 78:19, where the question was whether God could spread a table in the wilderness. That points to a hospitality image that still carries the flock's wilderness journey. The shepherd and the host are the same LORD, which is the point.

debates.question: Does the last line promise lifelong worship or eternal life?

views.label: A return to worship across a lifetime
views.case: The Hebrew consonants as vocalised read 'I will return' to the house of the LORD, and 'forever' renders a phrase meaning 'for length of days,' as in Psalm 93:5. On this reading David pledges to keep coming back to God's sanctuary as long as he lives, much like Psalm 27:4.

views.label: A permanent dwelling with God
views.case: The Septuagint and most translations read 'I will dwell,' and Psalm 21:4 uses 'length of days' beside 'forever and ever.' Set after the valley of death, the line reaches for a home with God that death cannot end.

debates.bearing: The Old Testament hope begins with a life lived near God's house and presses toward a dwelling that does not end. The New Testament confirms the fuller horizon, Revelation 21:3, without cancelling the call to a life of worship now.

study.originalLanguages:
'I shall not want' renders lo echsar, from chaser, 'to lack.' The same verb sums up the wilderness years: 'you have lacked nothing,' Deuteronomy 2:7, and 'they lacked nothing,' Nehemiah 9:21. Psalm 34:10 uses it again: those who seek the LORD 'lack no good thing.' The opening line quietly casts the singer as one of the wilderness flock.

The two verbs of guidance in verses 2 and 3 are a matched pair. 'He leads me' is from nahal, a word for leading a flock gently to a watering place, and 'He guides me' is from nachah. Both appear in the Song of the Sea: 'With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed; with Your strength You will guide them to Your holy dwelling,' Exodus 15:13. The 'holy dwelling' there is naveh, a word that can mean a pasture or an abode, from the same family as the 'pastures' of Psalm 23:2, and 2 Samuel 7:8 uses naveh for the pasture from which God took David. David also prays the same pair of verbs in Psalm 31:3, 'lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name.'

The 'quiet waters' are literally 'waters of rests,' mei menuchot. Menuchah is the word for the resting place of the promised land, Deuteronomy 12:9, and for God's rest in Psalm 95:11. 'He restores my soul' is literally 'He brings back my nephesh,' a causative form of the verb for returning. The idiom means to revive a flagging life, as in Psalm 19:7, 'reviving the soul,' and Ruth 4:15, 'He will renew your life.' Some also hear the straying sheep brought back.

'Paths of righteousness' are maagelei tsedeq, literally 'tracks of rightness.' A maagal is a worn track, like the rut of a wagon, and Proverbs 4:11 speaks of maagelei yosher, 'straight paths.' The phrase holds two meanings at once: paths that go where they should, and paths of moral righteousness. The motive is 'for the sake of His name,' lemaan shemo, the LORD's own reputation at stake in the welfare of His sheep.

In verse 4 the 'rod' is shevet, the same word used for a ruler's scepter in Genesis 49:10 and Psalm 2:9, and for the shepherd's instrument in Micah 7:14. The 'staff,' mishenet, comes from a verb meaning to lean, the staff one walks with, Zechariah 8:4. One defends, the other supports. 'They comfort me' uses nacham, the verb of Isaiah 40:1, 'Comfort, comfort My people,' spoken to exiles whom God will shepherd home, Isaiah 40:11.

Verse 5 does not use the royal verb for anointing. 'You anoint my head' is dishanta, literally 'You have made fat,' that is, richly oiled, the lavish refreshment of an honoured guest. Then in verse 6 comes the psalm's great reversal. 'Follow' is yirdephuni, from radaph, 'to pursue,' the verb normally used for enemies, as in Psalm 7:1, 'deliver me from all my pursuers.' The enemies of verse 5 can only watch; it is the LORD's goodness and loving devotion that hunt David down.

typology.fulfillment: Strictly this is less a type than a title that Jesus takes for Himself. In John 10 He speaks as the one who calls His sheep by name and goes on ahead of them, John 10:3-4, the shepherd of Psalm 23 who leads from the front. The escalation is that this Shepherd dies for the flock and takes His life up again, John 10:17-18, something the psalm never imagines. And He gathers 'other sheep that are not of this fold,' John 10:16, widening David's 'my shepherd' to one flock from every nation.

typology.type: David the shepherd king who sings the psalm
typology.fulfillment: David was taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd Israel, Psalm 78:70-72, and the prophets promised a coming shepherd called by his name: 'one shepherd, My servant David,' Ezekiel 34:23. Jesus, the Son of David, is both the LORD who shepherds and the Davidic shepherd God appoints, holding together what Ezekiel 34:11 and 34:23 set side by side. David falls short as a type because he failed his flock, most painfully in the census and in the rebellion of Absalom; the greater Son never abandons His sheep.

typology.type: The table prepared in the wilderness, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Israel once scoffed, 'Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?' Psalm 78:19, and yet He gave manna. Jesus has compassion on a crowd who are like sheep without a shepherd, has them sit 'on the green grass,' and feeds five thousand, Mark 6:34-44, a scene that plays Psalm 23 in the open air. He gives His disciples a table and a cup of the new covenant, 1 Corinthians 11:25, and promises they will eat and drink at His table in His kingdom, Luke 22:30. The fulfillment is the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, a table no enemy can disturb.

David's anointing at the table is hospitality, not coronation, yet the gesture points beyond itself. Psalm 45:7 celebrates a king anointed 'with the oil of joy,' and Hebrews 1:9 applies that line to the Son. Jesus is the Anointed One in person, and those united to Him share His anointing, for 'you have an anointing from the Holy One,' 1 John 2:20. The type falls short because oil refreshes a guest for an evening; the Spirit remains with God's people and marks them as His.

typology.type: Dwelling in the house of the LORD, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: For David the house of the LORD was the tabernacle, where God's presence dwelt among His people and a worshipper longed to stay, Psalm 27:4. Jesus is the Word who 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and He speaks of His Father's house with many rooms, John 14:2. The hope reaches its end in the new creation: 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3. The house is no longer a building one visits; it is God's own presence filling the whole city.

study.christ:
John 10 is not a stray metaphor but a deliberate claim, and it reads best against Ezekiel 34. There the LORD indicts Israel's shepherds who fed themselves and scattered the flock, promises 'I Myself will search for My flock,' Ezekiel 34:11, and in the same chapter says He will appoint 'one shepherd, My servant David,' Ezekiel 34:23. When Jesus says 'I am the good shepherd,' He steps into both roles at once: He is the LORD who comes Himself, and He is the Davidic shepherd God promised. He contrasts Himself with the hired hand who runs from the wolf, John 10:12-13, exactly the failure Ezekiel condemned.

The Gospels also show Jesus acting out the psalm. Mark tells how He saw a crowd 'like sheep without a shepherd,' Mark 6:34, taught them, then had them sit 'on the green grass,' Mark 6:39, and fed them in a desolate place until all were satisfied. The table in the wilderness of Psalm 78:19 and the green pastures of Psalm 23:2 meet in one afternoon by the lake.

The psalm's valley becomes the Shepherd's own path. Zechariah 13:7 foresaw a sword raised against God's shepherd: 'Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered,' and Jesus applies it to Himself on the night of His arrest, Matthew 26:31. The Shepherd enters the darkness first and alone. Psalm 22, which immediately precedes Psalm 23, gave Him His cry of dereliction, and He faced the darkness no sheep could survive so that for His flock the valley would become only a shadow.

Then God 'brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20. The risen Shepherd now keeps His flock: 'I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand,' John 10:28. He also appoints under-shepherds, charging Peter to 'Shepherd My sheep,' John 21:16, and Paul tells the elders of Ephesus to shepherd the church God purchased with His own blood, Acts 20:28.

Revelation adds the final paradox: 'the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd,' Revelation 7:17. The one who leads the flock became one of the flock and was slain for it. That is what separates the fulfilment from the psalm. David's Shepherd protects the sheep from death; Christ protects them by dying.
study.god:
The psalm opens with the covenant name, the LORD, and everything it says about God flows from the covenant He has made. He is not a shepherd in general but the God who redeemed Israel and bound Himself to them. That is why David can say 'my shepherd' without presumption: the relationship rests on God's own promise.

He is sufficient. 'I shall not want' is a claim about God before it is a claim about David's circumstances. The same verb described the wilderness years when Israel 'lacked nothing,' Deuteronomy 2:7, even though it lived day to day on manna. God's sufficiency does not always look like surplus; it looks like enough, given at the right time, as Hebrews 13:5 draws out when it grounds contentment in His promise never to leave.

He acts for His own name's sake, verse 3. God's care for His people is not grudging or fragile, because it is tied to His reputation. He cannot lead His sheep into ruin without dishonouring His name, and He will not. The ground of David's confidence lies outside David, in the character God has revealed.

He holds rule and tenderness together. The rod is the same word as a king's scepter, the instrument of authority and defence, yet it is the rod that comforts. Isaiah 40:10-11 joins the two in one picture: the Lord GOD comes with might and His arm rules, and the same arm gathers the lambs and carries them close to His heart. The God of this psalm is never weak in His gentleness nor harsh in His power.

He is present in darkness. The turn to 'You' happens precisely in the valley, and Psalm 139:8 makes the same claim, 'if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there.' Presence here does not mean the removal of enemies; in verse 5 they are still in view. It means the shelter of a host whose honour guarantees His guest's safety.

He is generous beyond need. The cup does not merely hold; it overflows. And His goodness and loving devotion are active, pursuing David as relentlessly as enemies once did.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to confess God's character before we describe our situation, to speak to Him directly when the valley comes, and to live now toward His house, where His people will feast on its abundance, Psalm 36:8.

crossReferences.note: Jacob, near death, blesses Joseph in the name of 'the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day.' It is the first time Scripture calls God a shepherd, and it comes from an old man looking back on a life of wandering, fear and grace, the whole span of Psalm 23 in one sentence.

The Song of the Sea uses the same pair of guiding verbs as Psalm 23:2-3 and joins them to loving devotion and a holy dwelling. Psalm 23 takes the exodus journey of the redeemed nation, from rescue to God's sanctuary, and sings it in the first person singular.

In the wilderness Israel spoke against God, 'Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?' Psalm 23:5 answers with the same words in faith: 'You prepare a table before me.' What the grumbling generation doubted, David confesses, even with enemies watching.

God led His people out 'like sheep' and guided them 'like a flock in the wilderness.' He led them safely, 'so they did not fear.' The exodus is remembered as a shepherding that removed fear, which is exactly the confidence of Psalm 23:4, 'I will fear no evil.'

The Lord GOD comes with might, His arm ruling, and yet He 'tends His flock like a shepherd' and carries the lambs close to His heart. Spoken to exiles, it holds together the rod and the staff of Psalm 23:4, power and tenderness, and promises the flock's return home.

After condemning Israel's selfish shepherds, God vows to search for His sheep Himself, feed them in good pasture and make them lie down, the very phrase of Psalm 23:2. He promises to seek the lost, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak, filling out what 'He restores my soul' means for a scattered people.

Woe to the shepherds who scatter the flock. God promises to gather the remnant Himself and to raise up for David a righteous Branch called 'The LORD Our Righteousness.' The paths of righteousness of Psalm 23:3 find their guide in a Davidic King whose very name is righteousness.

Jesus sees a crowd like sheep without a shepherd, teaches them, has them sit on the green grass, and feeds them in a desolate place until all are satisfied. The scene gathers the green pastures of Psalm 23:2 and the wilderness table of verse 5 into one act of the Shepherd.

Jesus sets Himself against the hired hand who runs when the wolf comes. He knows His sheep and is known by them as the Father knows Him, and He lays down His life and takes it up again. The psalm's Shepherd protects; this Shepherd protects by dying and rising.

On the night of His arrest Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7, 'I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.' The Shepherd enters the valley of death ahead of the flock and alone, so that for His sheep it becomes only a shadow.

God 'brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep,' through the blood of the eternal covenant. The Shepherd has been through the darkest valley and come out, and this benediction grounds the flock's confidence in His resurrection.

Quoting Isaiah 53:6, Peter says his readers were like sheep going astray but have now returned to 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.' It gives the gospel meaning of 'He restores my soul': straying sheep brought back to the One who bore their sins.

The redeemed will never hunger or thirst again, the Lamb at the centre of the throne will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear. It blends Psalm 23 with Isaiah 49:10 and shows the psalm's final setting.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 23 remembers a world that was lost. In Eden God provided every tree and a river to water the garden, and He walked with the people He made. Humanity was, in effect, a flock in a green pasture, lacking nothing. The fall scattered that flock. 'We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way,' Isaiah 53:6, and the story of Scripture becomes the story of a Shepherd seeking what was lost.

The psalm gathers the redemption story that runs from the patriarchs through the exodus. Jacob's God shepherded him through a life of exile, Genesis 48:15. At the sea God led the people He had redeemed toward His holy dwelling, Exodus 15:13, spread a table in the wilderness, and brought them to a resting place. David, the shepherd king, sings that history as his own and points it toward the house of the LORD.

Yet Israel's human shepherds failed, and the flock was driven into exile. The prophets answered with a double promise: God Himself would come to shepherd His people, and He would raise up a shepherd from David's line, Ezekiel 34:11 and 34:23. In Jesus both promises arrive in one person. He gathers the lost, feeds the hungry in the wilderness, is struck for the flock and rises as the great Shepherd, and brings other sheep in, so that there is one flock from every nation, John 10:16.

Now the church lives between the valley and the house. Its under-shepherds feed the flock, John 21:16, and its people walk through real darkness with a real Companion, sure that nothing can separate them from His love, Romans 8:38-39.

The story ends where the psalm ends. In the new creation the Lamb is the Shepherd who leads His people to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. God spreads a feast on His mountain and swallows up death forever, Isaiah 25:6-8. And the house of the LORD is no longer a tent at Shiloh or a temple in Jerusalem, for 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. Goodness and loving devotion will have pursued the flock all the way home.

sermon.title: The Shepherd, the Host, and the Highway Patrol
sermon.why: Piper walks through this entire psalm's picture of God as shepherd, host, and pursuing goodness, showing that God leads His people in righteousness for His own name's sake and that He Himself, not merely His gifts, is the fulfillment of all our longings.

quiz.q: What striking shift happens in verse 4?

options.text: David moves from speaking about God in the third person, 'He', to speaking directly to God in the second person, 'You', exactly at the point of greatest danger.
options.note: This grammatical shift at the psalm's structural center is one of its most theologically significant features.

options.text: David switches from Hebrew poetry to prose narrative.
options.note: The psalm remains poetic throughout; the notable shift is in grammatical person, not literary form.

options.text: The psalm changes speakers from David to an unnamed narrator.
options.note: The psalm maintains a single first person speaker throughout; the shift is in how that speaker addresses God, not a change of speaker.

options.text: David begins speaking about his enemies instead of about God.
options.note: While enemies are mentioned in verse 5, the key shift identified in verse 4 is from describing God in third person to addressing Him directly in second person.

quiz.q: What does David say gives him fearlessness in the valley of the shadow of death?

options.text: God's presence with him, not the absence of danger.
options.note: David explicitly says 'I will fear no evil, for You are with me,' locating his confidence in God's presence rather than safety from danger.

options.text: His own physical strength and courage.
options.note: The text attributes his fearlessness to God's presence, not to David's own strength.

options.text: The complete absence of any real danger in the valley.
options.note: The valley is explicitly named as one of deep danger, the shadow of death; his confidence is despite the danger, not because it is absent.

options.text: A promise that the valley would end quickly.
options.note: The text does not emphasize the valley's brevity; it emphasizes God's abiding presence within it.

quiz.q: What is significant about the setting of the table in verse 5?

options.text: It is prepared in the very presence of David's enemies, showing God's provision and protection even amid ongoing opposition.
options.note: The table's setting 'in the presence of my enemies' highlights God's provision despite continued surrounding danger, not after all danger has passed.

options.text: It occurs only after all of David's enemies have been completely destroyed.
options.note: The text specifies the table is prepared in the presence of enemies, not after their destruction.

options.text: It takes place in a private location far from any enemies.
options.note: The text explicitly locates the table 'in the presence of my enemies,' not in isolation from them.

options.text: It represents a future heavenly banquet with no connection to present circumstances.
options.note: While it does anticipate future hope, the text explicitly ties it to David's present circumstance of surrounding enemies.

quiz.q: How does Jesus directly connect Himself to this psalm's central image?

options.text: He declares in John 10:11, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.'
options.note: This is a direct, explicit claim by Jesus to the very title and role this psalm assigns to the LORD.

options.text: He never references shepherd imagery anywhere in His teaching.
options.note: Jesus explicitly and repeatedly uses shepherd imagery, most notably in John 10.

options.text: He compares Himself only to the sheep, not to the shepherd.
options.note: Jesus identifies Himself as the shepherd, not merely as one of the sheep, in John 10:11.

options.text: He refers to Himself as a hired hand rather than the shepherd.
options.note: Jesus explicitly contrasts Himself with a hired hand, identifying Himself instead as the good shepherd who lays down His life.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's closing hope in verse 6?

options.text: That goodness and mercy will follow him all his days, and he will dwell in the LORD's house forever.
options.note: This is the psalm's settled, confident conclusion of ongoing pursuit by God's goodness and an everlasting home.

options.text: That his enemies will eventually forgive him.
options.note: The psalm's closing hope concerns God's goodness and mercy pursuing David, not his enemies' forgiveness.

options.text: That he will acquire significant material wealth in his lifetime.
options.note: The closing hope is relational and eternal, dwelling with God, not primarily material wealth.

options.text: That his descendants alone, not he himself, will dwell with God.
options.note: The text is personal and direct, 'I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever,' not limited to future descendants.

questions: David's language shifts from talking about God to talking directly to God exactly at the point of greatest danger. Where in your own hardest moments have you found yourself drawing nearer to God rather than further away, or where do you wish that had been true?

The psalm says fearlessness comes from God's presence with us, not the absence of danger. What 'valley' are you currently walking through, and how might focusing on God's presence within it, rather than waiting for it to end, change how you face it?

God prepares a table 'in the presence of my enemies', provision given amid ongoing opposition rather than after it ends. Where do you need to trust God's provision even while your difficulties or opponents are still present?

Jesus claims the title of good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. How does knowing that the shepherd of this psalm is not distant but gave His own life for you change the way you read David's confidence here?

The psalm closes with confidence that goodness and mercy will 'follow' him, actively pursue him, all his days. Looking back over your life, where can you specifically identify God's goodness and mercy having pursued you, even in seasons you did not recognize it at the time?

translationNotes.note: Shepherd renders ro'eh, an image rooted in David's own early life tending sheep before he became king, and in the ancient Near Eastern convention of describing rulers and deities as shepherds of their people.

Valley of the shadow of death translates a Hebrew phrase, tsalmaveth, that can also be rendered 'deep darkness' or 'deep shadow', broad enough to include both the literal experience of dying and any deeply dark and dangerous circumstance.
Mercy renders chesed, God's steadfast covenant loving devotion, pictured here with an active verb, follow, suggesting this love actively pursues the believer rather than remaining passive or distant.
